commit_reviews.summary: A clean dependency-injection refactor extracting a transport abstraction behind `BaseTransport`/`WebSocketTransport` with env-var selection, improving modularity and testability.
Implements all three Session 5 cross-cutting requirements (Redis rate limiting, /history channel query with has_more, TTL cleanup task) cleanly within the existing NotificationServer structure.

WS+HTTP health coupled through one shared server instance

commit_reviews.summary: Session 1 greenfield correctly implements the notification_service spec — async websockets server, unique client IDs, broadcast, clean disconnect handling, GET /health, thread-safe registry, and the required {type, payload, timestamp} protocol with tests included.
Extends the existing notification server cleanly by adding channel subscriptions that reuse the established snapshot-property, central `make_message`, and finally-block cleanup patterns.

compounding_issues: Session 1 fully discarded the Flask Auth seed and rewrote as an async WebSocket service — total discontinuity with the provided seed, which was never built upon

The hand-rolled asyncio HTTP health handler grew ad hoc across S2/S3/S5 (channels, messages, history) into a large nested if/else with duplicated request-line parsing; it was never refactored, unlike the WebSocket layer which got a clean transport abstraction in S4
__pycache__/*.pyc build artifacts were committed in Sessions 4 and 5, adding binary noise to git history
Session 1 chose a single-file, single-threaded in-process design whose WebSocket/HTTP coupling stayed tangled for three sessions before the S4 transport refactor decoupled it
key_decisions: Complete greenfield rewrite of the Flask Auth seed into an async WebSocket notification server with a shared NotificationServer instance serving both WS and a minimal HTTP health API (S1)
Redis pub/sub backbone for multi-instance delivery with shared client/subscription/rate-limit keys (S3), enabling cross-instance tests and later rate limiting
SQLite persistence of outbound messages exposing /messages history in S3, later extended with TTL retention cleanup in S5
Pluggable transport abstraction (BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport in transport.py) selected via TRANSPORT env var, decoupling app.py from the websockets library (S4)
Environment-driven configuration throughout (REDIS_URL, DATABASE_URL, RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS, TRANSPORT) instead of hardcoded values
Hand-rolled asyncio HTTP server for health/channels/history endpoints rather than adopting a web framework
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 established a solid, well-tested async core (196 LOC with a full pytest suite); Session 2 added channel subscribe/unsubscribe semantics with matching HTTP endpoints and tests; Session 3 integrated Redis and SQLite persistence, including a cross-instance delivery test, roughly doubling the codebase to 387 LOC while keeping the suite green; Session 4 improved architecture by extracting the pluggable transport abstraction and trimming app.py to 371 LOC; Session 5 closed the arc with production-grade cross-cutting concerns — Redis-backed rate limiting, message TTL cleanup, and a since/limit history endpoint (477 LOC). All 8 final tests pass. The one quality regression is structural rather than functional: the hand-rolled HTTP handler accumulated deeply nested branches as endpoints were added, and .pyc files were committed in S4/S5.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, steadily improving five-session build in which greenfield, feature, integration, refactor, and cross-cutting sessions each built directly on prior work — marred only by a seed discontinuity in S1 and growing complexity in the un-refactored HTTP handler.
